endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Verification and validation activities should encompass both the clinical user and the environment in which the AI system is implemented, including factors such as whether the solution is properly installed, instructions for use are correct, and software safety elements work properly (i.e., user acceptance testing [UAT]).

endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: the developers should provide training materials (eg, tutorials, manuals, examples) and/or training activities (eg, hands-on sessions) in an accessible format and language, taking into account the diversity of end users

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Supporting resources such as AI fact sheets, model cards (such as the CHAI Applied Model Card), or solution documentation should remain accessible to staff between formal training cycles for self-directed review, if interested.

endorsements.title: Training for tomorrow: Establishing a worldwide curriculum in online adaptive radiation therapy
endorsements.issuer: Technical innovations & patient support in radiation oncology
endorsements.quote: One approach is to develop structured, modular training programs that can be customised to different regions, taking into account local resources, local jurisdiction limitations, MDT make up, and technological capabilities.

endorsements.title: Current challenges for global equity related to the implementation of artificial intelligence in pediatric imaging
endorsements.quote: Procurement should require local-language user interface (UI), instructions for use, and training materials.

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Sufficient-quality ultrasound scans with versus without in-app tutorial videos
evidence.effect: Sufficient scans: 85.3% with tutorials versus 43.2% without (OR: 14.1, 95% CI: 6.40–31.12, p < 0.001). App version was confounded with facility; data combined remote-review and AI-supported workflows.
evidence.quote: Bivariate results showed a strong positive association between the use of an app with tutorial videos and scan quality (OR: 14.1, 95% CI: 6.40–31.12, p < 0.001).

commentary.bottom_line: One observational study from Sierra Leone found that sufficient-quality obstetric ultrasound scans rose from 43.2% to 85.3% when in-app tutorial videos were available, but app version was confounded with facility. The evidence suggests that accessible training materials may improve correct tool use, though certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: A single cross-sectional study in real deployment tests the practice. It reports an odds ratio of 14.1 (95% CI 6.40 to 31.12) for sufficient scans with tutorials. Confounding of app version with facility, mixed remote-review and AI-supported workflows, and one setting lower certainty to very low. The wide interval also signals imprecision.

Insufficient-quality scans can lead to missed or delayed obstetric findings or to AI outputs based on poor inputs. The study measured scan quality, an intermediate outcome, and did not report maternal or neonatal harm. Whether tutorials prevent errors from reaching patients remains untested.

The tutorials were embedded in the app, so providers met them inside the workflow rather than in separate sessions. The study covered 81 providers across 7 facilities and 2,315 scans. It did not measure how often providers watched the videos or how long tutorials took, so fidelity and burden are unknown.

The only test took place in rural Sierra Leone with providers working in non-English or limited-English contexts. This matches the endorsements' emphasis on local-language materials. No test examined Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users in the United States, so transfer to those groups is uncertain.

The study did not report the cost of producing, translating, or maintaining tutorial videos, nor staff time spent on training. Health systems weighing adoption at scale have no supplied data on resource needs, and the five endorsing sources rely on expert judgment rather than cost analysis.

commentary.research_gap: No controlled study compares tailored, multilingual training and reference documentation against standard materials with facility confounding removed. Future studies should measure patient outcomes, user error rates, tutorial uptake, and costs, and they should test materials matched to different expertise levels and languages in health systems in the United States.
commentary.underserved_note: The single test included rural, limited-English or non-English providers in Sierra Leone, which supports relevance to language-diverse users. It did not include Medicaid, safety-net, or explicitly low-literacy populations in the United States, so health systems serving those groups should treat the finding as indirect.
